items.readable_text:
Content:
The notation [MATH: \textrm{cis}\,\theta] is a compact way of writing complex numbers given in polar form. Under this notation, the number [MATH: \textrm{cis}\,\theta] corresponds to

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{cis}\,\theta = \cos\theta+ \textrm{i} \sin \theta.]

Content:
For example, consider the following complex number:

Content:
[MATH: z =\cos \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + \textrm{i} \sin \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} \right)]

Content:
Let's write this number using [MATH: \textrm{cis} \, \theta] notation. Here, [MATH: \theta = \textrm{arg}\,(z)= \dfrac{\pi}{3}.] Therefore, we get

Content:
[MATH: z = \textrm{cis} \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right).]

Content:
Similarly, consider the complex number

Content:
[MATH: w = 5\left[\cos \left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) + \textrm{i} \sin \left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6} \right)\right].]

Content:
Let's write this number using [MATH: \textrm{cis} \, \theta] notation as well. In this case, [MATH: \theta = \textrm{arg}\,(w)= \dfrac{5\pi}{6}.] Therefore, we get

Content:
[MATH: w = 5\,\textrm{cis} \left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The number [MATH: \textrm{cis}\,\theta] corresponds to

[MATH: \textrm{cis}\,\theta = \cos \theta + \textrm{i}\sin \theta.]

Therefore, we get

[MATH: 4cis((π)/(6))|= 4[\cos ((π)/(6)) + \textrm{i}\sin ((π)/(6))]; = 4[(sqrt(3))/(2) + \textrm{i}((1)/(2))]; = 2sqrt(3) + 2\textrm{i}.]

sections.normalized_html: Express [MATH: z=-\sqrt{3}+\textrm{i}] using the [MATH: \textrm{cis}] notation.
sections.readable_text: Express [MATH: z=-\sqrt{3}+\textrm{i}] using the [MATH: \textrm{cis}] notation.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Computing the magnitude [MATH: |z|,] we get

[MATH: |z||= sqrt((− sqrt(3))^{2} + 1^{2}); = sqrt(3 + 1); = sqrt(4); = 2.]

Now, since [MATH: z] lies in the second quadrant, we can find the argument [MATH: \textrm{arg}(z)] as follows: [MATH: \arg (z)|= π − \arctan|(y)/(x)|; = π − \arctan|(1)/(− sqrt(3))|; = π − \arctan ((1)/(sqrt(3))); = π − (π)/(6); = (5π)/(6)]

Therefore,

[MATH: z = -\sqrt{3}+\textrm{i}= 2\,\textrm{cis}\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right).]

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: z_1=5\textrm{cis}\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)] and [MATH: z_2=3\textrm{cis}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right),] calculate the product [MATH: z_1z_2.]
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: z_1=5\textrm{cis}\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)] and [MATH: z_2=3\textrm{cis}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right),] calculate the product [MATH: z_1z_2.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To compute the product of two complex numbers [MATH: z_1 = r_1\textrm{cis}\,\theta_1] and [MATH: z_2 = r_2\textrm{cis}\,\theta_2,] we use the formula

[MATH: z_1z_2 = r_1 r_2\,\textrm{cis}\left(\theta_1 + \theta_2\right).]

Substituting [MATH: r_1 = 5,] [MATH: r_2 = 3,] [MATH: \theta_1 = \dfrac{5\pi}{6},] and [MATH: \theta_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{3},] we get

[MATH: z_{1}z_{2}|= 5 ⋅ 3 ⋅ cis((5π)/(6) + (π)/(3)); = 15cis((7π)/(6)).]

By expanding the [MATH: \textrm{cis}] notation and evaluating the sine and cosine, we can get the expression in Cartesian form:

[MATH: z_{1}z_{2}|= 15cis((7π)/(6)); = 15[\cos ((7π)/(6)) + \textrm{i}\sin ((7π)/(6))]; = 15[− (sqrt(3))/(2) + \textrm{i}(− (1)/(2))]; = − (15)/(2)(sqrt(3) + \textrm{i})]

Substituting [MATH: r_1 = 5,] [MATH: r_2 = 3,] [MATH: \theta_1 = \dfrac{5\pi}{6},] and [MATH: \theta_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{3},] we get

By expanding the [MATH: \textrm{cis}] notation and evaluating the sine and cosine, we can get the expression in Cartesian form:

[MATH: z_{1}z_{2}|= 15cis((7π)/(6)); = 15[\cos ((7π)/(6)) + \textrm{i}\sin ((7π)/(6))]; = 15[− (sqrt(3))/(2) + \textrm{i}(− (1)/(2))]; = − (15)/(2)(sqrt(3) + \textrm{i})]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To compute the quotient of two complex numbers [MATH: z_1 = r_1\textrm{cis}\,\theta_1] and [MATH: z_2 = r_2\textrm{cis}\,\theta_2,] we use the formula

[MATH: \dfrac{z_1}{z_2} = \dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\,\textrm{cis}\left(\theta_1 - \theta_2\right).]

Substituting [MATH: r_1 = 3,] [MATH: r_2 = 9,] [MATH: \theta_1 = \dfrac{3\pi}{4},] and [MATH: \theta_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{2},] we get

[MATH: (z_{1})/(z_{2})|= (3)/(9)cis((3π)/(4) − (π)/(2)); = (1)/(3)cis((π)/(4)).]

By expanding the [MATH: \textrm{cis}] notation and evaluating the sine and cosine, we can get the expression in Cartesian form:

[MATH: (z_{1})/(z_{2})|= (1)/(3)cis((π)/(4)); = (1)/(3)[\cos ((π)/(4)) + \textrm{i}\sin ((π)/(4))]; = (1)/(3)[(sqrt(2))/(2) + \textrm{i}(sqrt(2))/(2)]; = (1)/(6)(sqrt(2) + sqrt(2)\textrm{i})]
sections.readable_text:

Substituting [MATH: r_1 = 3,] [MATH: r_2 = 9,] [MATH: \theta_1 = \dfrac{3\pi}{4},] and [MATH: \theta_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{2},] we get

[MATH: (z_{1})/(z_{2})|= (3)/(9)cis((3π)/(4) − (π)/(2)); = (1)/(3)cis((π)/(4)).]

By expanding the [MATH: \textrm{cis}] notation and evaluating the sine and cosine, we can get the expression in Cartesian form:

[MATH: (z_{1})/(z_{2})|= (1)/(3)cis((π)/(4)); = (1)/(3)[\cos ((π)/(4)) + \textrm{i}\sin ((π)/(4))]; = (1)/(3)[(sqrt(2))/(2) + \textrm{i}(sqrt(2))/(2)]; = (1)/(6)(sqrt(2) + sqrt(2)\textrm{i})]

[MATH: \arg (z)|= π − \arctan|(y)/(x)|; = π − \arctan|(1)/(− sqrt(3))|; = π − \arctan ((1)/(sqrt(3))); = π − (π)/(6); = (5π)/(6)]

[MATH: z = -\sqrt{3}+\textrm{i}= 2\,\textrm{cis}\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right).]

Explanation:
To compute the product of two complex numbers [MATH: z_1 = r_1\textrm{cis}\,\theta_1] and [MATH: z_2 = r_2\textrm{cis}\,\theta_2,] we use the formula

[MATH: z_1z_2 = r_1 r_2\,\textrm{cis}\left(\theta_1 + \theta_2\right).]

Substituting [MATH: r_1 = 5,] [MATH: r_2 = 3,] [MATH: \theta_1 = \dfrac{5\pi}{6},] and [MATH: \theta_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{3},] we get

[MATH: z_{1}z_{2}|= 5 ⋅ 3 ⋅ cis((5π)/(6) + (π)/(3)); = 15cis((7π)/(6)).]

By expanding the [MATH: \textrm{cis}] notation and evaluating the sine and cosine, we can get the expression in Cartesian form:

[MATH: z_{1}z_{2}|= 15cis((7π)/(6)); = 15[\cos ((7π)/(6)) + \textrm{i}\sin ((7π)/(6))]; = 15[− (sqrt(3))/(2) + \textrm{i}(− (1)/(2))]; = − (15)/(2)(sqrt(3) + \textrm{i})]

Item 13 — Example: Evaluating a Quotient of Complex Numbers Expressed in CIS Notation

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: z_1=3\textrm{cis}\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)] and [MATH: z_2=9\textrm{cis}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right),] calculate the quotient [MATH: \dfrac{z_1}{z_2}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To compute the quotient of two complex numbers [MATH: z_1 = r_1\textrm{cis}\,\theta_1] and [MATH: z_2 = r_2\textrm{cis}\,\theta_2,] we use the formula

[MATH: \dfrac{z_1}{z_2} = \dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\,\textrm{cis}\left(\theta_1 - \theta_2\right).]

Substituting [MATH: r_1 = 3,] [MATH: r_2 = 9,] [MATH: \theta_1 = \dfrac{3\pi}{4},] and [MATH: \theta_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{2},] we get

[MATH: (z_{1})/(z_{2})|= (3)/(9)cis((3π)/(4) − (π)/(2)); = (1)/(3)cis((π)/(4)).]

By expanding the [MATH: \textrm{cis}] notation and evaluating the sine and cosine, we can get the expression in Cartesian form:

[MATH: (z_{1})/(z_{2})|= (1)/(3)cis((π)/(4)); = (1)/(3)[\cos ((π)/(4)) + \textrm{i}\sin ((π)/(4))]; = (1)/(3)[(sqrt(2))/(2) + \textrm{i}(sqrt(2))/(2)]; = (1)/(6)(sqrt(2) + sqrt(2)\textrm{i})]
